name: Ben Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I'm not much of a talker about this stuff, but go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at the grocery distribution centre out on the ring road, ten at night till half six. I'm in the chilled section, so it's yoghurt, milk, meat, all at about three degrees, and you wear a fleece under your hi-vis all year. A voice in the headset tells me which aisle and how many, I say the check number back, and I build the cage for the store. The pick rate is what wears you out, they want about 180 cases an hour and the scanner on your wrist shows if you're behind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, if anything?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The lads on my shift, honestly. There's Dev and Marek and we have our break at three in the morning with the vending machine coffee, and it's a laugh. And I know the chilled aisles with my eyes shut now, eight years in. I don't love the job, but I know it, and I know what my money will be every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it was all talk. At break I'd probably say the bosses were the ones who believed it, not us. Online I don't post much, maybe I'd share something from the union page saying jobs are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I'm still on £11 and something an hour on nights with nothing in the bank. Nothing changing isn't great for me either, because nothing changing means rent goes up and my wages don't. Amira and I are always about two weeks from payday trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, that's the plan. I'd do the Saturday overtime when it comes up, which is about one in three weeks. I'd stay in the union because if there's a pay round I want to be counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit flat, really. Relieved there's no robot coming, but tired just thinking about the same rent and the same rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would be first to get tight in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, because I need it for nights, there's no bus at ten at night out to the ring road. If the car needs a part, that's the month gone. Last winter the exhaust went and I borrowed £200 off Amira's mum, which I hated doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's Amira, for anyone reading this later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira's my girlfriend, we live together in a one-bed above the chip shop on Station Road. She works at the care home on days, so we see each other mostly at weekends. If the warehouse work stays the same, that doesn't change either.

say: I'd tell the night shift it was **all talk** and the bosses fell for it.
I'd share the **union's post** saying warehouse jobs are safe.
think: Nothing changing still means **rent rises** and my nights pay doesn't.
My partner and I are always about **two weeks** from payday trouble.
do: Keep turning up on **nights** and keep my head down on the pick rate.
Take the **Saturday overtime** whenever it comes round, about one week in three.
Stay in the **union** so I'm counted when there's a pay round.
feel: Relieved there's **no robot** coming, but flat about the same rent and rota.
S0.quote: Nothing changing isn't great for me either, because nothing changing means rent goes up and my wages don't.
fieldNote: His job feels **safe** here, but the money worry was already there before AI came up.
The **car** is the weak point: no bus to the night shift, so one repair wipes out a month.
He borrowed from his **partner's mum** last winter and still feels bad about it.

steps.text: Keep working the chilled night shift and take Saturday overtime
Keep paying union dues so he's counted in the pay round

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get in early and get it in writing that nobody gets sacked for a robot. I'd say it at break and I'd sign whatever petition goes round. The office lot will feel it first, that's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think the headset voice even needs a person in the office any more in that world, so the planning lads upstairs go first. Then they start trialling robots on the ambient side, the dry goods, and we're the test after that. I've seen the videos of those robot arms picking tins. I reckon I've got a few years, but I'm not the type who's going to learn to fix those robot arms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting, that's the main thing, and push for a deal on no compulsory redundancies. I'd try to put £20 a week aside, even if it means no takeaway on Fridays. I wouldn't do any computer course, I'd be wasting their money and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's going a bit soft under me. Not panicking yet, but I'd be checking the noticeboard every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a course. What if the company offered one, paid, on the clock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably go, because it's paid and I'd look bad saying no. But I'd be the one at the back, I know that about myself. Dev would be the one who actually gets something out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's fine for now, which is half true. She'd see through it, she always does. She'd probably say the care home is always hiring, and I'd say I'm not doing nights wiping people, and we'd have a row about it.

say: I'd tell everyone the **union** has to get no-sackings promises in writing early.
I'd say the **office planners** will feel it first, not us on the floor.
think: The **ambient side** gets robot trials first, and the chilled aisles are next.
I've got **a few years**, but I'm not going to learn to fix the machines.
do: Go to every **union meeting** and push for no compulsory redundancies.
Put **£20 a week** aside by dropping the Friday takeaway.
Skip any **computer course** unless the company pays for it on the clock.
feel: Like the **floor's going soft** under him, checking the noticeboard every shift.
S1.quote: I reckon I've got a few years, but I'm not the type who's going to learn to fix those robot arms.
fieldNote: He expects robots on his floor within **a few years**, and doesn't see himself moving with them.
He leans hard on the **union** as his whole plan, more than on anything he'd do himself.
Admits he'd go to a **paid course** but sit at the back; honest about his own resistance.

steps.text: Attend every union meeting and push for no compulsory redundancies
Put £20 a week into savings by dropping Friday takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, tax the companies that use robots and pay people. I'd go to a march if there was one. At work I'd say they can't just switch us off like a light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I think I'm done by 2031. The office goes in 2028, which means the pick rates get set by a machine that never sleeps and the managers with it. Then three years later the robots come for the cages. I've got no savings, no other skill, and there's only two big sheds near us and they'd both do it at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, that's the honest answer. I'd stay in the union and go on whatever march there is. I'd probably sign up for the government help the day it exists. Past that I've got nothing, I'd just keep picking till they tell me not to come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like when you get a letter from the landlord and you don't want to open it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots don't come till 2031 in this picture. Does those three years change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, shouldn't it. Three years, I could do a forklift ticket or something. But forklifts are robots too by then, aren't they, so what's the point. I'd probably waste the three years worrying and doing overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Amira cut first, if your hours started going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, which means I can't get to nights, which means I lose the job anyway. That's the trap. We'd probably have to ask her mum about moving into her back room, and I'd rather sleep in the car.

say: I'd say the **government** must tax robot-using firms and pay the people pushed out.
I'd go on any **march** and say they can't switch us off like a light.
think: I think I'm **done by 2031**, with no savings and no other skill.
Both **big sheds** near us would bring the robots in at the same time.
do: Stay in the **union** and join whatever march gets organised.
Sign up for **government help** the day it exists.
Keep picking and doing **overtime** until they tell him not to come in.
feel: Sick, like an **unopened letter** from the landlord he doesn't want to read.
S2.quote: I've got no savings, no other skill, and there's only two big sheds near us and they'd both do it at the same time.
fieldNote: No plan at all beyond the **union** and benefits; he says so plainly.
Sees the **three-year gap** before robots but thinks forklift work goes too, so would waste it.
The **car trap** is real: lose the car, lose the night shift, lose the job.

steps.text: Join any union march for a robot tax
Apply for government income support as soon as it opens
Keep picking on nights and take every overtime shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before really, the union has to fight it, and I'd say the politicians have five years so there's no excuse. I'd share stuff online about a robot tax. I'd say it louder than I say things now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, I'll be honest. I'd be 32 when the thinking part lands and about 35 when the robots get to the cages. That's still young enough. Five years, I could start something else in theory, but in practice I'd sit on it till year four, because that's what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get Amira and me to save properly, maybe £30 a week, which would be about £1,500 a year. I'd look at the care home thing she keeps going on about, maybe do a couple of shadow shifts. And I'd vote for whoever says they'll make the companies pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick, more nagging. Like a toothache you keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the care home thing was a row in the last picture. What's changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, that's what's changed. With two years I'd just dig in, with five I'd have to admit care work is the one thing they can't put a robot in, or not soon. I still don't fancy it, wiping people, but Amira does it and she's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually do it rather than sit on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody making me, honestly, the union or a mate going first. If Dev went and did a care course I'd go. I don't move first, I never have.

say: I'd say the **politicians** have five years, so there's no excuse to do nothing.
I'd share posts online for a **robot tax** and say it louder than now.
think: I'd be **35** when robots reach the cages, still young enough in theory.
I'd probably **sit on it** till year four, because that's what I do.
do: Save about **£30 a week** with his partner, around £1,500 a year.
Do a couple of **shadow shifts** at the care home where his partner works.
Vote for whoever promises to make **companies pay**.
feel: Less sick, more of a **nagging toothache** he keeps putting off.
S3.quote: Five years, I could start something else in theory, but in practice I'd sit on it till year four, because that's what I do.
fieldNote: The extra time moves him from no plan to a **reluctant** one: care work through his partner.
Says outright he only moves when **someone else goes first**.
Still expects to **lose the job**; the time only changes what he might do after.

steps.text: Save £30 a week with his partner towards a £1,500 cushion
Do two shadow shifts at the care home on his days off
Vote for candidates who back a tax on robot-using firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to get proper retraining going, paid, not some online thing. I'd say that in the union meetings. Online I'd say the same, it's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and three, so about 2039 for the robots. I'd be 40. That actually feels far, which is the problem, because I know I'd let it slide. But the job would go in the end, and the pay wouldn't go up on the way there either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on nights for now, because the money's slightly better. I'd try to do a care certificate over a couple of years if the union got it paid. I'd keep going to meetings. Probably wouldn't save much, to be honest, because there's nothing left over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not scared. More like something I'd think about at three in the morning by the vending machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self, starting at the warehouse at nineteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the forklift ticket and do some evening class, anything. I thought the warehouse job would just always be there. It's been there eight years and it's the same pay as when I started near enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the robots came for the chilled aisles in 2039, who would you worry about most on your shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, because he's older, he'd be near 60 by then. I'd be all right-ish if I'd moved by then. Marek can't lift a resident in a care home with his back.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for **paid retraining**, not some online thing.
I'd tell the **union meetings** it's on the government to sort it.
think: The robots come around **2039**, when I'd be 40, which feels far.
I know I'd **let it slide**, and the job would still go in the end.
do: Stay on **nights** for the slightly better pay while it lasts.
Do a **care certificate** over two years if the union gets it paid.
Keep going to **union meetings**, though saving much isn't realistic.
feel: Uneasy but **not scared**, a worry for three in the morning at the vending machine.
S4.quote: I thought the warehouse job would just always be there. It's been there eight years and it's the same pay as when I started near enough.
fieldNote: Even with a decade he expects to **lose the job**, and his money gives him nothing to plan with.
The worry he names is for **Marek**, the older colleague, more than himself.
Regrets not doing a **forklift ticket** or evening class at nineteen.

steps.text: Stay on the chilled night shift for the extra pay
Take a two-year care certificate if the union gets it funded
Keep attending union meetings about paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. There's no time and no money and I'd just be picking till they tell me not to come in. What would help is the company having to keep paying us while we retrain, a proper wage, because I can't do a course on nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the car. Everybody talks about robots, nobody talks about the fact that you can't get to these sheds without a car. If they built a bus out to the ring road, half of us would have £150 a month more.

headlineQuote: You can't get to these sheds without a car. If they built a bus out to the ring road, half of us would have £150 a month more.
portrait: **Ben** is 27 and has picked chilled groceries on nights for **eight years**, living with his partner above a chip shop.
He has under a month saved, and the **car** he needs for nights is his biggest money risk.
He leans left and puts his faith in the **union** and government rather than his own moves.
He knows he's **slow to change** and admits he'd wait for a mate to go first.
He goes from uneasy in the plateau to **panicked** if AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time, no money and no other skill to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** at a real wage, plus a **bus** out to the ring road sheds.
